McKinsey Montreal hackathon · Track 2 / Housing affordability

Housing analysis and app

Where is rent eating Montreal's renters alive, who is most exposed, and what could we ship in a 2-hour Cursor session to do something about it?
Source data: Statistics Canada (StatsCan) 2021 Census Profile (Catalogue 98‑401‑X2021013) and the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) 2025 Rental Market Report (RMR). Bundle: 02_housing/housing_data.zip (151 MB) — extract and run python analysis.py && python gis_analysis.py && python correlations.py. All figures in this document are produced by those three scripts. Acronyms are expanded on first use throughout; the two terms that recur most are defined below.

Two terms used throughout

Forward Sortation Area (FSA)
A forward sortation area (FSA) is a way to designate a geographical unit based on the first three characters in a Canadian postal code. Canada Post groups every postal code into one of about 1,640 FSAs nationally, and Statistics Canada publishes Census tables at the FSA level. This document analyses 196 FSAs in the Montreal area (postal codes starting with H, J3T, J3X, J3Z, or J4 through J7) using StatsCan's 2021 Census Profile.
Shelter-cost-to-Income Ratio (STIR)
The share of a household's pre-tax income spent on shelter (rent or mortgage, plus utilities, plus property tax for owners). The conventional Canadian thresholds are 30 percent (cost-burdened) and 50 percent (severely cost-burdened). The headline metric used in this document, pct_tenant_stir30, is the percentage of tenant households in a given FSA that spend 30 percent or more of household income on shelter.

01

Executive summary

Montreal renter cost-burden in 2021 was already concentrated and structural. The headline metric is the Shelter-cost-to-Income Ratio (STIR), the share of household income spent on shelter; a household at STIR of 30 percent or more is conventionally classed as cost-burdened. Across 192 Montreal-area FSAs with material renter populations, 67 have at least 30 percent of their renters cost-burdened. The five most stressed FSAs are concentrated downtown: H3B at 63.5 percent (the financial district anchored by Place Ville Marie and the Bell Centre), H3A at 61.4 percent (McGill University and the Golden Square Mile), H3G at 55.3 percent (the Concordia Sir-George-Williams campus around Guy-Concordia metro), J7B at 54.8 percent (the Mirabel / Saint-Janvier suburban belt, a small-sample outlier), and H3H at 53.8 percent (Shaughnessy Village near Atwater metro). CMHC's 2025 RMR shows the picture has worsened sharply since: average rents grew 10.9 percent between October 2024 and October 2025 across the CMA, while incomes have grown roughly 12 percent since the 2020 reference year. The 2021 figures should be read as a floor.

Findings

  • The downtown cluster is a single contiguous problem. H3A, H3B, H3G, and H3H form one zone within 4 km of McGill and Concordia universities, sharing five characteristics: high rent, modest renter income, large tenant populations, single-digit subsidised-housing share, and student-heavy demographics. The fact that they are spatially adjacent matters — it means one coordinated municipal response can cover all of them.
  • Stress tracks rent, not income. Side-by-side maps of cost-burden, rent level, and household income (Section 03) show the stress geography lining up with the rent geography, not the income geography. This rules out an income-redistribution-only response: even meaningful wage gains would not close the gap if rents continue their CMHC-reported 10.9 percent annual climb.
  • Owner-side and renter-side affordability are different problems. Owner cost-burden tracks low income; renter cost-burden tracks high rent. They should be reported and acted on as two programs, not one.
  • The economic-activity and new-construction layers are still missing from this analysis (Section 04 sets them up). Joining building permits, CMHC starts, and Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) FSA-level tax data to the stress map is the next step. The diagnostic to compute is the three-way overlap: FSAs that are high stress + high economic activity + low new construction. Those are the policy bullseye — places where people work but cannot afford to live, and where supply is not catching up.

Opportunities

  • Coordinate a single municipal response on the downtown cluster. H3A through H3H ought to be governed as one tenancy zone in the Service de l'habitation's portfolio — uniform PSL eligibility rules, joint outreach with the comités logement at McGill and Concordia, and a shared 24-month rent-stabilisation pilot. Today the four FSAs span at least two arrondissements (Ville-Marie and Le Plateau-Mont-Royal in part) and are managed in parallel.
  • Re-audit OMHM and SHQ subsidy placement against current stress. The aggregate Pearson test was statistically null at FSA level; a unit-level audit of OMHM unit locations and SHQ Programme de supplément au loyer (PSL) allocations against the FSA stress ranking would surface whether subsidy is going where it is needed today. The audit is a one-quarter scope of work for the housing portfolio team.
  • Build where the economy is and supply is not. Use the building-permits dataset and CMHC Starts & Completions Survey (Section 04) to find FSAs in the top half of economic activity but the bottom quartile of housing starts. These are the FSAs where Ville de Montréal can fast-track zoning variances and where Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) Affordable Housing Innovation Fund money has the highest marginal return.
  • Close the CMHC asking-rent reporting lag. CMHC's RMR anchors to October survey rents, leaving a 12-to-24-month blind spot. App 4 in Section 05 (Rent Pulse Montréal) is the small ship to fix this; the policy benefit is that the next quarterly Housing Market Insights brief can carry a real-time signal, not a year-old one.
  • Stand up renter-side and owner-side dashboards separately. Conflating the two metrics in a single “housing affordability” chart hides the fact that they are driven by different variables and respond to different policies. App 1 and App 2 (Section 05) are the renter-side build; an analogous mortgage-stress tool for owner-side is a separate hackathon track.
02

The headline distribution

What does the spread of renter cost-burden look like across the city?

The 2021 distribution is long-tailed. The bulk of Montreal-area FSAs sit between 20 and 30 percent of renters cost-burdened — right at the conventional 30 percent stress threshold. The right tail is what matters: about 67 FSAs cross the threshold, and a smaller hardcore (16 FSAs) cross the “severe” line at 40 percent of renters burdened. There is no left tail to celebrate — even the best-performing suburban FSAs sit around 10 to 17 percent.

The policy target is not “reduce average stress.” It is “close the right tail” — bring the 16 severely-stressed FSAs back into the bulk distribution. Most of those are within 4 km of McGill and Concordia universities.

03

Geographic Information System (GIS) view — where the stress lives

195 of 196 Montreal-area FSAs joined to the StatsCan 2021 FSA boundary shapefile (lfsa000b21a_e). Projection used for the maps: EPSG:32188, the European Petroleum Survey Group (EPSG) identifier for Modified Transverse Mercator (MTM) zone 8 — the local north-up projection for Montreal.
04

Economic activity and new construction — the bullseye layer

The stress map answers where the pain is. Two further layers answer where the jobs are (Canada Revenue Agency tax statistics by FSA) and where supply is growing (Ville de Montréal building permits plus CMHC Starts and Completions). All three datasets are now downloaded, joined, and visualised below.

Joined to the FSA stress map, these layers turn an affordability diagnostic into a siting tool. The three-way overlap — high renter stress, high economic activity, low new construction — is the policy bullseye. The composite ranking surfaces ten FSAs that meet all three conditions; the worst three are H3C (Griffintown / Cité-du-Multimédia), H3X (Hampstead edge of Côte-Saint-Luc), and H3G (Concordia Sir-George-Williams campus).

Layer A — Where is the economic activity?

The cleanest FSA-resolved proxy for economic activity is the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) Individual Tax Statistics by FSA, which publishes the number of tax filers and total employment income per FSA, annually. StatsCan's Canadian Business Counts (Tables 33-10-1014 and 33-10-1016) publishes establishment counts but only at Census Metropolitan Area (CMA) and Census Subdivision (CSD) level — not FSA — so we use CRA as the FSA-resolution source. Caveat: the CRA measure is filer-side (where people live and file taxes), not workplace-side. For most Montreal FSAs the two correlate, but the financial district (H3B) and university FSAs (H3A around McGill, H3G around Concordia) will under-count by this measure because their daytime workplace populations are not their residents.

Layer B — Where is new construction happening?

Two complementary sources cover Montreal. The Ville de Montréal building-permits dataset is the operational source: 1,661 aggregated records 1990 through 2026, by arrondissement (borough) by year by permit type. The CKAN application programming interface (API) endpoint returns the data directly. Aggregated to 2020 through 2024 construction permits (permit code CO), it shows where the city's permit activity is concentrating in the post-pandemic supply response. The CMHC Starts and Completions Survey (via Statistics Canada Table 34-10-0156) gives the macro CMA-level monthly time series.

The bullseye — stress × economic activity × construction

Each FSA receives three percentile ranks: renter cost-burden (stress), CRA economic-activity score (number of filers times average filer income), and an inverted permit-volume rank for its arrondissement (lower permits is worse, since stress + economy + low supply is the bullseye condition). The composite bullseye score is the sum of the three ranks, capped at 3.0. Ten FSAs cross 1.85 on the composite. The visualisation below plots all 185 matched FSAs on the stress (y) by income (x) plane, sized by their arrondissement's 2020 through 2024 permit volume and coloured by the composite rank.

The H3G / H3H / H3C / H3X cluster is the operational priority. H3G (Concordia campus) and H3H (Shaughnessy Village) are both in the renter-stress top-10 already; H3C (Griffintown / Cité-du-Multimédia) and H3X (Hampstead / western Côte-Saint-Luc edge) only surface once economic activity is brought in. The arrondissement-level permit data shows Ville-Marie (which contains H3G, H3H, H3C, H3A, H3B) issuing $2.2 billion of permit value over 2020 through 2024 in only 1,454 permits — high-dollar, low-unit construction. The Subsidy Gap Finder app (Section 05, App 2) and the Three-Way Bullseye pitch (Section 05, App 5) operationalise this directly.
05

App concepts — what to ship in a hackathon

For renters

STIR-Score Montréal

Pre-rent advisory. Type your postal code, your monthly rent, and your income — get your stress score, your FSA's median, and a templated letter you can send a landlord with comparable-FSA rent data attached as anchoring evidence.
Data sources
  • StatsCan Census 2021 FSA profile (already in bundle) — median rent, median income, percent cost-burdened per FSA.
  • CMHC RMR 2025 Table 1.1.2 — current asking rents by zone, mapped to FSA via Census Tract crosswalk.
  • StatsCan Postal Code Conversion File (PCCF) — converts the user's six-character postal code to its FSA and Dissemination Area (DA). Free, refreshed monthly.
  • Société de transport de Montréal (STM) and exo General Transit Feed Specification (GTFS) feeds (optional) — power the “FSA peers with similar transit access but lower rent” recommendation.
  • User input — rent, income, household size. No account required.
In-app Actions
  • Real-time STIR computation and severity badge: green below 30 percent, amber 30 to 40 percent, red 40 percent or above.
  • Show your dot on your FSA's renter distribution, plotted as a kernel density estimate (KDE).
  • “What if” sliders: a 10 percent rent shock or a 10 percent income shock — mirrors the CMHC year-over-year scenario.
  • Peer-FSA recommender: three FSAs within 4 km with similar transit time and lower median rent.
  • Severity-aware copy: above 40 percent STIR triggers a soft escalation to the resources panel for the Regroupement des comités logement et associations de locataires du Québec (RCLALQ).
Outbound Triggers
  • Generate landlord letter — PDF (Portable Document Format) with a comparable-FSA rent table from CMHC and StatsCan, signed and dated, ready to email.
  • Email STIR memo to self — for budgeting and mortgage broker conversations.
  • Calendar reminder — iCalendar (ICS) file: “review your rent against the CMHC October release” 60 days before lease anniversary.
  • One-click handoff to the nearest comité logement (member organisation of RCLALQ, the Québec network of tenants' rights clinics) if severity is red, with a pre-filled intake form.
  • Share anonymised score on Reddit r/montreal or as a screenshot, as an opt-in community pressure signal.
Stack: Streamlit + affordability_tabulations.csv + the PCCF + ReportLab for the PDF letter. Total lines of code (LOC): about 300. Hosting: free Streamlit Cloud tier.
For Ville de Montréal and the Office municipal d'habitation de Montréal (OMHM)

Subsidy Gap Finder

A 2-D map of every FSA plotted on a stress-by-subsidy grid that lets the housing portfolio manager click into quadrants and see which FSAs are over-served and which are starving. Triggers a real workflow action — a draft reallocation memo and a portfolio-team ticket.
Data sources
  • mtl_fsa_joined.geojson (produced by gis_analysis.py) — FSA polygons, STIR, and subsidy share, in one file.
  • OMHM annual report — current subsidised-unit count per arrondissement (borough); the PDF table requires an annual scrape.
  • Société d'habitation du Québec (SHQ) Programme de supplément au loyer (PSL) allocations — rent-supplement units by borough, published quarterly.
  • Rôle d'évaluation foncière (Ville de Montréal open data, the municipal property assessment roll) — vacant-lot and under-utilised parcel inventory for siting decisions.
  • CMHC RMR quarterly updates — feed the gap-score refresh cadence.
In-app Actions
  • Quadrant filter on a stress (Y) by subsidy (X) scatter; bubble area is tenant population.
  • Click an FSA to open a drawer with its 21 Census metrics, polygon outline, and top-three demographic summary.
  • “Gap score” ranking equals STIR percentile minus subsidy percentile, ranging from minus 100 (over-served) to plus 100 (under-served).
  • Diff mode: compare the current quarter against the prior CMHC release.
Outbound Triggers
  • Generate reallocation memo — a 2-page Word document (.docx) briefing OMHM's executive on the top-five underserved FSAs (for example, the H3A, H3B, H3G, H3H cluster), with implied unit shortfall and candidate parcels from the rôle foncière.
  • Create a portfolio ticket — POST to OMHM's internal Jira or SHQ workflow tool: “Investigate PSL allocation in H3A, gap-score plus 62.”
  • Export CSV ranked by gap-score for the monthly portfolio review.
  • Notify on movement — an email digest when any FSA's gap-score shifts by more than 10 points after a CMHC quarterly release.
  • Public dashboard publish — one-click push of an anonymised summary to donnees.montreal.ca for accountability.
Stack: Folium + GeoPandas + mtl_fsa_joined.geojson + python-docx + the Jira REST application programming interface (API). About 500 LOC. Hosting: Ville de Montréal's internal Cloud.gc.ca tenancy.
For the Front d'action populaire en réaménagement urbain (FRAPRU), the comités logement (local tenants' rights clinics), and other community organisations

Stress Cluster Alert

A community-organising dashboard that intersects renter stress with demographic vulnerability — one-parent families, recent immigrants, seniors — to find FSAs where economic stress is compounding with social fragility. Triggers operational outputs: canvassing assignments, opt-in SMS (short message service) blasts, press-release drafts.
Data sources
  • mtl_fsa_census_subset.csv with the KEEP_IDS list extended to additional StatsCan characteristic identifiers (IDs):
    • One-parent family share (ID approximately 78)
    • Recent immigrant share, 5-year arrivals (ID approximately 1142)
    • Population aged 65 and older as a share (ID approximately 13)
    • Visible minority share (ID approximately 1325)
  • mtl_fsa_joined.geojson — polygons plus STIR for the spatial filter.
  • Centraide of Greater Montreal vulnerability index (public aggregated dataset) — cross-check.
  • FRAPRU member-organisation SMS opt-in list — private CSV, FSA-tagged.
In-app Actions
  • Pick one to three demographic dimensions; the dashboard live-recomputes a compound-vulnerability score per FSA.
  • Ranked list of stress clusters with the contributing dimensions visible.
  • Map overlay: stress polygons tinted by compound score.
  • “Drill into FSA” view: demographic-mix bar chart plus historical comparison (against the 2016 Census where available).
Outbound Triggers
  • Print canvassing brief — one-page PDF per FSA: demographics, top concerns, nearest community centre, doorstep script in French and English.
  • Push canvassing assignment to an Airtable or Notion volunteer roster via REST API: “Saturday June 21, FSA H3A team, four volunteers needed.”
  • Bulk SMS via Twilio to opted-in renters in a stress-cluster FSA with a tenants'-rights information link.
  • Press-release draft auto-generated when a new severe-stress and compound-vulnerability FSA appears quarterly.
  • Slack webhook into FRAPRU's internal channel when a previously-amber FSA crosses into red.
Stack: Flask + Leaflet + Twilio API + Airtable API + WeasyPrint for the PDFs. About 700 LOC. Hosting: a $5-per-month Hetzner virtual machine; SMS is the only marginal cost.
For CMHC and other market analysts

Rent Pulse Montréal

CMHC's RMR lags real-market rents by about two years and about 30 percentage points: rents grew roughly 30 percent since 2020 while the survey still anchors to 2021 Census shelter cost. This app closes the lag by pairing CMHC's October 2025 official rents with continuously-scraped asking-rent listings. Outputs feed the next CMHC quarterly publication directly.
Data sources
  • Centris.ca — the Multiple Listing Service (MLS) feed operated by the Québec Centris-affiliated real estate boards (the umbrella body abbreviated QCAR). Legal API access requires a partnership; this is the gold-standard source for asking-rent comparables.
  • Kijiji and Facebook Marketplace — scraped listings, FSA-tagged via address geocoding (Nominatim).
  • Inside Airbnb Montreal — quantifies long-term housing siphoned to short-term rentals per FSA.
  • CMHC RMR Table 1.1.2 (already in bundle) — baseline reference for the lag computation.
  • StatsCan PCCF — address resolves to FSA, which resolves to CMHC zone.
In-app Actions
  • Weekly heat-map: dollars-per-month lag (asking median minus CMHC official) per FSA.
  • Time-series view per zone: the CMHC anchor point plus a rolling 4-week asking-rent median.
  • Distribution view: histogram of asking rents within a zone with the CMHC mean marked.
  • Anomaly tracker: FSAs whose median asking-rent moved more than 5 percent week-over-week (WoW).
Outbound Triggers
  • Weekly PDF brief auto-emailed to a CMHC analyst distribution list (GitHub Actions cron plus Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, SMTP).
  • API push to CMHC's internal market-monitoring dashboard with current lag per zone.
  • Microsoft Teams notification on any FSA whose median asking-rent moves by more than 5 percent WoW.
  • CSV input formatted to the next CMHC Quarterly Housing Market Insights brief schema.
  • Flag to the Tribunal administratif du logement (TAL) — auto-forward listings priced more than 50 percent above the CMHC zone median to the TAL outreach team as potential illegal-rent-hike candidates.
Stack: scrapy + sqlite + Nominatim + pandas + ReportLab + GitHub Actions cron + SMTP. The scraping is the only hard part; everything downstream is pandas plus the CMHC zones CSV from the bundle. About 1,000 LOC.
06

Reproducibility

Everything in this document was produced from housing_data.zip.

The bundle 02_housing/housing_data.zip (151 MB) contains:

  • data/mtl_fsa_census_subset.csv — 196 Montreal FSAs by 21 metrics, filtered from StatsCan's national 645 MB Census Profile CSV (Comma-Separated Values file, Catalogue 98-401-X2021013).
  • data/cmhc_rmr_montreal_2025.xlsx — CMHC 2025 RMR for the Montreal CMA. The Message Digest 5 (MD5) hash was verified against a fresh download from the CMHC URL on 2026-06-17.
  • data/fsa_boundaries/lfsa000b21a_e/ — StatsCan 2021 FSA digital boundary shapefile (1,643 polygons, 297 MB uncompressed).
  • data/meta.txt — the StatsCan codebook used to pivot the Census long-form data.
  • MANIFEST.md — provenance and a one-command reproduction recipe.

Recipe:

cd ~/Desktop/mck_hackathon_montreal/02_housing
unzip -o housing_data.zip
python3 analysis.py
python3 gis_analysis.py
python3 correlations.py
open housing_analysis_and_app.html

End-to-end, the three scripts produce three CSV files (affordability_tabulations.csv, cmhc_zone_rents.csv, correlations_matrix.csv), seven PNG figures, and one GeoJSON (mtl_fsa_joined.geojson) — all consumed by this report.

07

Appendix — correlation matrix

What the matrix shows:

  • Strong, expected, and partly definitional: rent versus the cost-burden share at r equals +0.72. Since rent is the numerator of the STIR ratio, a positive correlation is mechanically guaranteed; the value above 0.7 still adds information by quantifying how tightly the two move together.
  • Real and independent: owner-side stress against household income at r equals -0.44. Owner cost-burden is an income-side problem, distinct from the rent-driven renter problem.
  • Statistically null: subsidised-housing share against renter cost-burden at r equals -0.10, with p equals 0.18 at n equals 192. The Spearman rank correlation gives the same value, so the null is robust to outliers. The implication is operational: a direct audit of OMHM unit locations against the FSA stress ranking would resolve whether subsidy is currently well-targeted; the aggregate test alone cannot.
StatsCan, 2021 Census of Population, Catalogue 98-401-X2021013 (Forward Sortation Areas) and 92-179-X (FSA Boundary File). CMHC, 2025 Montreal Rental Market Report. McKinsey Montreal Cursor Hackathon — pro bono analysis. Produced 2026-06-17.
